transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Novapay CTO), Aisha Patel (Novapay ML Eng), Samir Gupta (Novapay Infra), Lina Torres (Novapay PM)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync - throughput optimization. Focus on continuous batching, concurrency and queueing.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick roll call, and then Priya will walk through the latest runs.
[00:12] Michael Chen: Yeah thanks, Jordan. All here from Novapay. Trying to keep this short — we, um, have a big payment event next month so throughput matters.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Totally, that's what we're focusing on. Priya, over to you.
[00:25] Priya Rao: Cool. I sent the new spreadsheet earlier — it's the batch-concurrency matrix. We ran three main profiles: low-latency (single-token opt for 64 tokens), typical (128 tokens), and long (256 tokens). Each profile tested batch sizes 8/16/32 and concurrency 10/50/100/200.
[00:42] Aisha Patel: Quick question, is concurrency here client-side concurrent requests or concurrent model workers?
[00:47] Priya Rao: Good call. It's client concurrency hitting the frontend, which maps to simultaneous requests in the Redwood runtime; we also measured backend worker concurrency separately. Some naming mismatch in the sheet, sorry.
[01:05] Priya Rao: High-level: at up to ~150 qps we see good p50 and p95, but when we push above ~300 qps with concurrency >100 we start seeing the p99 spike and timeouts; looks like queueing backpressure at the request router.
[01:22] Samir Gupta: To be clear, those timeouts are at the app layer or from the GPU worker? We saw a few 504s.
[01:26] Priya Rao: Mostly at the router layer — requests waiting in the inbound queue; once queued they sometimes expire before getting a batch formed on the GPU. The KV cache and prefix caching is helping for repeated prefixes, but this workload has heavy variability so cache hit is low.
[01:42] Jordan Lee: Right, and remember we can adjust queue timeout, max in-flight per worker, and the continuous batching window. Those are the levers.
[01:52] Michael Chen: Can you explain continuous batching again? I thought batching only happens on the GPU when enough requests arrive.
[01:57] Priya Rao: Yeah so continuous batching maintains an open micro-batch for a short window (like 10-50ms) to collect requests and form a larger batch even with low immediate QPS. It trades a little extra client latency for much better throughput and GPU utilization. We saw 30-50% token-cost reduction in our last runs when we enabled it for 128-token workloads.
[02:18] Aisha Patel: Hmm 50% sounds good but p99 is our killer metric. What happened to p99 when you enabled continuous batching?
[02:24] Priya Rao: Good question — p99 moved slightly up when we enabled a larger batching window at very high concurrency because requests waited longer in the queue. But with tuned max concurrency and a shorter batching window (20ms) we got p99 back to acceptable range while keeping higher throughput.
[02:42] Lina Torres: What's acceptable range again? For us p99 needs to be under 600ms end-to-end for the payment flow.
[02:48] Jordan Lee: Correct, Novapay target is sub-600ms p99.
[02:52] Priya Rao: In the tuned run we got p99 ~520ms for 128-token typical workload at 350 qps with continuous batching=20ms and max_concurrency=120.
[03:05] Samir Gupta: When you say max_concurrency 120 is that per worker or cluster-wide?
[03:09] Priya Rao: That's cluster-wide for the frontend router; per-worker in-flight was 8. So we limited the router to not overload workers.
[03:18] Michael Chen: We saw CPU spikes on the router pods during the higher tests. Any config to smooth that?
[03:24] Priya Rao: We can scale router horizontal replicas and tune the accept queue depth. Also, batching reduces CPU per request because fewer scheduling ops per token. But you'll need to ensure router pod autoscaling or manual replica count to handle peak accept rates.
[03:37] Jordan Lee: One other knob is the batch packing policy — prioritize latency-sensitive requests into small micro-batches and background jobs into larger ones. That helps keep p99 bounded.
[03:48] Aisha Patel: Is that priority packing something we can configure today?
[03:51] Priya Rao: Yes, it's in the routing policy. We can tag requests with priority header; Redwood runtime will attempt to form micro-batches for high-priority tags and larger batches for lower-priority. Priya: we can demo that packing in the next call.
[04:05] Priya Rao: Also, for this POC we recommended a target concurrency sweet spot between 80-140 for your typical 128-token workload — below that you underutilize GPUs, above that queueing becomes painful.
[04:17] Michael Chen: Makes sense. The tricky part is our traffic bursts — 10x bursts for a few minutes. How does Redwood handle sudden ramp?
[04:25] Priya Rao: We saw two behaviors: if you have headroom (extra router replicas and worker capacity) the runtime will absorb bursts. If you're at capacity, fallback policies kick in — you can fall back to a smaller model variant or degrade to lower token generation. There's also graceful drop policies.
[04:40] Jordan Lee: Note: for Dedicated you can reserve burst capacity so you don't get throttled across other tenants.
[04:46] Samir Gupta: Any measurable difference between hosted and dedicated here for throughput?
[04:51] Priya Rao: Dedicated gives you predictability and reserved GPU pools. For throughput it's more about configuration — but dedicated avoids noisy neighbors and offers higher quotas for concurrency. We saw consistent p99 improvements when the trial was on dedicated nodes.
[05:05] Michael Chen: Good. Can you run through the specific benchmark numbers in the sheet?
[05:09] Priya Rao: Sure. I'll read the highlights: profile A (128 tokens) at qps target 350, batch 16, concurrency 120 -> p50 45ms, p95 180ms, p99 520ms, token cost 0.028 per 1k tokens (approx in our cost model). With batch 32 we improved cost but p99 went to 760ms due to extra queueing.
[05:35] Aisha Patel: So batch 32 improves cost but breaks p99. Is mixing batches per priority the recommended approach?
[05:40] Priya Rao: Yes, pack latency-sensitive into smaller batches. Also, we can set a max wait time so batches flush sooner if a request is hitting p99 thresholds.
[05:50] Jordan Lee: I recommend for Novapay: continuous batching=20ms, max_concurrency=120, per-worker in-flight=8, pack priority headers for payments, and maintain at least 2x router replicas for bursts.
[06:05] Lina Torres: That config looks reasonable. What's the impact on cost if we maintain those settings?
[06:10] Priya Rao: We'll attach the cost delta in the sheet — rough ballpark: about 10-20% higher than the absolute cheapest config but keeps p99 under 600ms; cheaper configs push p99 above target.
[06:22] Michael Chen: For the ramp test we want to simulate peak events: can Redwood run a synthetic load or should we run it from our side?
[06:29] Jordan Lee: We can run a coordinated load test with you. Best practice is you run it from your environment so you test ingress and network e2e; we can provide a harness and helper scripts.
[06:40] Samir Gupta: We'll likely run from our infra — will share IP ranges and request patterns.
[06:47] Priya Rao: When you share the pattern, we'll pick initial config and watch metrics (queue depth, batch sizes, p99) and suggest incremental tuning.
[06:56] Aisha Patel: Any gotchas around KV cache — we noticed cache misses spike during bursts.
[07:01] Priya Rao: If your request prefixes vary a lot, cache hit will be low. We can apply prefix normalization for payment IDs and that usually improves KV cache hit. Also, increasing cache size helps but has memory cost.
[07:14] Michael Chen: Regarding timeouts — we saw a few 30s timeouts in the logs. Are those client-side or router-side?
[07:20] Priya Rao: Those are upstream timeouts; we should correlate app logs. Likely the request queued longer than the client's socket timeout. We'll surface guidance on socket timeouts vs internal queue timeouts.
[07:32] Jordan Lee: Ok quick pivot — Lina, any timeline constraints for the pilot?
[07:36] Lina Torres: We want this ramp validated by Oct 27 so we can lock config for the payment event on Nov 3.
[07:42] Jordan Lee: Good — that matches our suggested schedule.
[07:45] Priya Rao: I'll run two targeted experiments: one shorter window (20ms continuous batching) and one with priority packing. Expect results by 10/22.
[07:55] Michael Chen: Great. And Jordan will send pricing?
[07:58] Jordan Lee: Yes, I'll follow up with Dedicated reservation options and cost delta for the tuned config.
[08:03] [08:03] (brief side conversation about calendar invites)
[08:10] Priya Rao: I also wanted to flag an observation: in one run the router's accept queue grew to 18k items before we scaled, which caused long tail. So automatic autoscaling triggers for router replicas are important.
[08:23] Samir Gupta: That's concerning — our autoscaler currently reacts on CPU and pod-level metrics, might be too slow for spikes.
[08:29] Priya Rao: We recommend a custom metric on queue depth and a faster scale policy (scale to target in 30-60s). Also consider warm reserved replicas during predicted windows.
[08:41] Michael Chen: If we reserve extra capacity, is there a cost jump?
[08:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, dedicated reservation will increase committed costs but reduces risk; we can show tradeoffs.
[08:50] Aisha Patel: One more tuning question — do we see different behavior with quantized models? We tested int8 variant.
[08:56] Priya Rao: Quantized runs lower GPU utilization per token and slightly faster per-token latency in some cases, but sometimes batching behavior changes because kernel choices differ. For your workload int8 had lower cost but p95 degraded in a couple of runs; needs more tuning.
[09:12] Lina Torres: Actionable ask: can you add the int8 runs into the shared spreadsheet with the same batching matrix?
[09:18] Priya Rao: Yes will do.
[09:20] Michael Chen: Ok, let's capture the core decisions.
[09:23] Jordan Lee: Recap: target config continuous batching 20ms, max_concurrency 80-140 (we'll tune to 120), per-worker in-flight 8, priority packing for payments, router replicas 2x baseline and queue-depth autoscaling. Priya to share updated results by 10/22, Novapay runs ramp test by 10/27, Jordan shares pricing and pilot SOW by 10/23.
[09:45] Aisha Patel: Sounds good. Small note: please include how to set priority headers in the SDK sample.
[09:51] Priya Rao: Will include code snippet.
[09:53] Michael Chen: Also please include recommended client socket timeout and server queue timeout pairs.
[09:57] Priya Rao: Adding that too.
[10:00] Jordan Lee: Great thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after the ramp test.
[10:03] Michael Chen: Thanks, bye.

(Transcript end)
